transcript.content:
This would be amazing if I could see it. I really hope the Moon is visible right now!

I'm in Davis, California, USA at 2026-08-14 14:00 PDT (UTC-0700) (2026-08-14T21:00:00Z in UTC), at latitude 38.5449 degrees and longitude -121.7405 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is 63.367 degrees and its azimuth is 206.962 degrees, so it is above the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 50.94 degrees and its azimuth is 157.604 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 5.95 percent illuminated, 28.172 degrees from the Sun, and 371351.1 kilometers away. The sky brightness is bright daylight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

To be honest, it would be **extremely difficult**, if not impossible, to see the Moon with your naked eyes under these specific conditions.

Here is the breakdown of why:

### 1. The "Daylight Washout" Effect
Even though the Moon is high in the sky (50.94 degrees), the Sun is also very high (63.367 degrees). Because the Sun is only about 28 degrees away from the Moon, they are in the same general area of the sky. 

When the Sun is that high, the atmosphere is flooded with scattered sunlight (Rayleigh scattering). This creates a high level of "sky brightness." The Moon, which is only 5.95% illuminated (a very thin crescent), does not have enough reflected light to compete with the overwhelming brightness of the blue sky.

### 2. The Phase of the Moon
At 5.95% illumination, you are looking at a very slender waxing crescent. While these are beautiful and easy to see during twilight (just after sunset or just before sunrise), they are much harder to see during the middle of the day. Because the "lit" portion of the Moon is so small, there isn't enough surface area reflecting light to stand out against the glare of the sun.

### 3. Contrast is Key
In astronomy, visibility is all about contrast. 
*   **At night:** The background is black, so even a dim object stands out.
*   **At 2:00 PM:** The background is bright blue/white. 

Because the Moon is so close to the Sun in this scenario, it will likely be "lost" in the glare. It’s similar to trying to see a dim flashlight beam while someone is pointing a high-powered stadium floodlight nearby.

### The Verdict
If you look toward the azimuth of **157° (roughly South-Southeast)**, you might see a very faint, ghostly "smudge" or a slight change in the texture of the sky if you squint perfectly, but for an ordinary observer with unaided eyesight, **it will likely be invisible.**

**Tip:** If you really want to see it, you would need a pair of **binoculars**. Even a basic pair would likely be enough to pull the crescent out of the daylight glare!
